title: ECG Essentials
summary: A systematic approach to the 12-lead ECG, the intervals that matter, and the territories that map to coronary arteries.

sections.heading: A systematic approach
sections.body: Read every ECG the same way, every time. The order matters less than the consistency — a system is what stops you from spotting the obvious abnormality and missing the important one.
facts: Check patient details, date, calibration (10 mm/mV) and paper speed (25 mm/s)
Rate: 300 divided by the number of large squares between QRS complexes, or count complexes in 10 seconds and multiply by 6 if irregular
Rhythm: regular or irregular; is there a P wave before every QRS and a QRS after every P?
Axis: look at leads I and aVF
P wave morphology and duration
Intervals: PR, QRS, QT and corrected QT
ST segments and T waves in every territory
Compare with a previous ECG whenever one exists

table.caption: Standard adult reference values
rows: Atrial depolarisation plus AV nodal delay
Plateau phase of the action potential

sections.heading: Coronary territories
sections.body: Mapping ECG leads to coronary arteries is one of the highest-yield pieces of knowledge in cardiology.

rows: Tall R and ST depression in V1–V3; confirm with V7–V9

sections.heading: Patterns worth recognising immediately
facts: ST elevation in contiguous leads with reciprocal depression — acute coronary occlusion
Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression — acute pericarditis
Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular rhythm — atrial fibrillation
Sawtooth flutter waves, classically at an atrial rate near 300 per minute — atrial flutter
Wide complex tachycardia with AV dissociation, capture or fusion beats — ventricular tachycardia
Short PR with a delta wave — ventricular pre-excitation
Tall tented T waves progressing to a sine wave — hyperkalaemia
Electrical alternans with low voltage — large pericardial effusion

pearls: A normal ECG never excludes coronary artery disease.
Always look for reciprocal change — it substantially increases confidence in ST elevation.
In inferior infarction, record right-sided leads: right ventricular involvement changes management.
Compare with an old ECG before calling anything 'new'.
Interpret the ECG in the context of the patient in front of you, not in isolation.

title: The Cardiac Cycle
summary: The sequence of pressure, volume, valve and electrical events that make up a single heartbeat.

sections.heading: Phases of the cycle
sections.body: The cycle is best learnt as a sequence of pressure relationships, because every valve event follows directly from a pressure crossover.
facts: Atrial systole: atrial contraction completes ventricular filling, contributing the final 10–30% (the atrial kick)
Isovolumetric contraction: ventricular pressure rises with all valves closed; no change in volume
Rapid ejection: ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure, semilunar valves open, most of the stroke volume is ejected
Reduced ejection: ejection continues more slowly as ventricular pressure begins to fall
Isovolumetric relaxation: semilunar valves close, all valves closed again, pressure falls steeply
Rapid filling: AV valves open, the majority of ventricular filling occurs passively
Diastasis: slow filling as atrial and ventricular pressures approach equilibrium

sections.heading: Volumes and derived measures
facts: End-diastolic volume: approximately 120 mL
End-systolic volume: approximately 50 mL
Stroke volume = EDV − ESV, approximately 70 mL
Ejection fraction = SV ÷ EDV, normally about 55–70%
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate, approximately 5 L/min at rest
Cardiac index = cardiac output ÷ body surface area, approximately 2.5–4.0 L/min/m²

rows: Large in tricuspid stenosis and pulmonary hypertension; absent in atrial fibrillation; cannon waves in AV dissociation
Atrial relaxation and downward movement of the tricuspid annulus
Tricuspid bulging in early ventricular systole
Atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve
Giant v waves in tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid opening and rapid ventricular filling
Prominent in constriction; blunted in tamponade

pearls: Every valve opens or closes because of a pressure crossover — never memorise valve events separately from pressures.
Most ventricular filling is passive; the atrial kick matters most when the ventricle is stiff or the rate is fast.
Coronary perfusion of the left ventricle happens in diastole, so tachycardia reduces supply while increasing demand.
Systole shortens far less than diastole as heart rate rises — diastole absorbs almost all the reduction.
The dicrotic notch on the aortic trace marks aortic valve closure.

title: Haemodynamics
summary: Preload, afterload, contractility and resistance — the four levers that determine cardiac output and arterial pressure.

sections.heading: The core equations
facts: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate
Mean arterial pressure = cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance
Mean arterial pressure ≈ diastolic pressure + one third of pulse pressure
Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic pressure
Systemic vascular resistance = (MAP − right atrial pressure) ÷ cardiac output
Stroke volume = end-diastolic volume − end-systolic volume

rows: End-diastolic volume; CVP or wedge pressure
The load the ventricle must overcome to eject
Systemic vascular resistance; aortic pressure; wall stress
Intrinsic force of contraction at a given load

sections.heading: Frank–Starling and Laplace
sections.body: Two principles explain most of clinical haemodynamics.
facts: Frank–Starling: increasing end-diastolic fibre length increases the force of contraction, up to a point
In heart failure the Starling curve is depressed and flattened, so extra filling raises pressure rather than output
Laplace's law: wall tension is proportional to pressure multiplied by radius, divided by twice the wall thickness
This is why a dilated ventricle works harder for the same pressure, and why hypertrophy normalises wall stress
It also explains why aneurysms grow progressively faster as they enlarge

sections.heading: Flow and resistance
facts: Poiseuille's law: flow is proportional to the fourth power of radius — halving the radius reduces flow sixteen-fold
Arterioles are the principal resistance vessels; veins are the capacitance vessels
The venous system holds roughly 60–70% of total blood volume
Pulmonary vascular resistance is roughly one tenth of systemic vascular resistance
Hypoxia constricts pulmonary vessels but dilates systemic ones

pearls: When output falls, work out which lever is broken: preload, afterload, contractility or rate.
Ejection fraction is load-dependent — it is not a pure measure of contractility.
The right ventricle is afterload-sensitive; the left ventricle tolerates pressure loading far better.
Venoconstriction increases preload without changing total blood volume.
In tamponade and right ventricular failure, preload reduction is harmful, not helpful.

title: Coronary Circulation
summary: How the heart feeds itself: anatomy, the diastolic nature of coronary flow, and the supply–demand balance that governs ischaemia.

sections.heading: Anatomy and dominance
facts: Left main coronary artery divides into the left anterior descending and left circumflex arteries
LAD supplies the anterior wall, anterior two thirds of the septum and the apex via septal and diagonal branches
Left circumflex supplies the lateral wall through obtuse marginal branches
Right coronary artery supplies the right ventricle, the inferior wall, and usually the AV node
Dominance is defined by the origin of the posterior descending artery: right in roughly 85%, left in about 8%, co-dominant in the remainder
Sinuatrial nodal artery arises from the RCA in about 60% of hearts and from the circumflex in the rest

sections.heading: Why coronary flow is diastolic
sections.body: During systole, contracting myocardium compresses intramural vessels. In the left ventricle this compression exceeds coronary driving pressure, so almost all left coronary flow occurs in diastole. The right ventricle, generating much lower pressure, has more evenly distributed flow.
facts: Coronary perfusion pressure = aortic diastolic pressure − left ventricular end-diastolic pressure
Tachycardia shortens diastole disproportionately and reduces perfusion time
The subendocardium is compressed most and perfused last, so it becomes ischaemic first
Anything that raises LVEDP — heart failure, aortic stenosis, ischaemia itself — reduces perfusion pressure

sections.heading: Flow regulation
facts: Myocardial oxygen extraction is 70–80% at rest — near maximal, so demand must be met by increased flow
Coronary flow reserve is the ratio of maximal to resting flow, normally about four- to five-fold
Local metabolites, especially adenosine and nitric oxide, dominate regulation over autonomic tone
Autoregulation maintains flow across a wide range of perfusion pressures
Fractional flow reserve compares distal to aortic pressure during maximal hyperaemia to judge functional significance

pearls: Learn one artery, one territory, one set of ECG leads — it pays off constantly.
Because extraction is already near-maximal, only increased flow can meet increased demand.
Angina can occur with entirely normal coronary arteries — in aortic stenosis, hypertrophy or microvascular disease.
Slowing the heart rate helps ischaemia twice over: less demand and more diastolic perfusion time.
Inferior infarction with bradycardia points to the right coronary artery and the AV node.

title: Heart Sounds & Murmurs
summary: What produces each sound, how to characterise a murmur, and the manoeuvres that tell murmurs apart at the bedside.

rows: Loud in mitral stenosis; soft in mitral regurgitation and long PR
Splits on inspiration normally; soft A2 in severe aortic stenosis; loud P2 in pulmonary hypertension
Rapid early diastolic filling into a compliant or volume-loaded ventricle
Normal in the young and in pregnancy; in older adults suggests heart failure
Atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle
Always abnormal in adults; suggests hypertrophy, ischaemia or fibrosis

sections.heading: Describing a murmur
facts: Timing: systolic, diastolic or continuous — and where within that phase
Site of maximal intensity and radiation
Character: harsh, blowing, rumbling, musical
Intensity: graded 1 to 6 for systolic murmurs, where grade 4 and above has a palpable thrill
Pitch: high-pitched murmurs are heard best with the diaphragm, low-pitched with the bell
Effect of respiration and of dynamic manoeuvres

rows: Left sternal edge, sitting forward in expiration

sections.heading: Dynamic manoeuvres
facts: Inspiration increases right-sided murmurs (Carvallo's sign); expiration increases left-sided murmurs
Valsalva strain reduces preload: most murmurs get quieter, but hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and mitral valve prolapse get louder
Squatting increases preload and afterload: HOCM and prolapse murmurs get quieter
Standing from squatting reduces preload: HOCM and prolapse murmurs get louder
Handgrip increases afterload: mitral and aortic regurgitation get louder; aortic stenosis gets quieter

pearls: Murmur intensity does not reliably indicate severity — a critically stenotic valve can be quiet.
Two murmurs get louder on Valsalva: hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and mitral valve prolapse.
In acute severe regurgitation the murmur may be short or absent — never rely on it to exclude the diagnosis.
An S3 in an older adult is one of the most useful bedside signs of raised filling pressures.
Feel the carotid while you listen: it anchors you in the cardiac cycle.

title: Arrhythmia Principles
summary: The three mechanisms behind every arrhythmia, and a framework for classifying rhythms at the bedside.

sections.heading: Three mechanisms
facts: Re-entry: a circuit with unidirectional block and slow conduction sustains a self-perpetuating wavefront. Accounts for most clinical tachyarrhythmias — AVNRT, AVRT, atrial flutter, scar-related VT
Enhanced automaticity: abnormal spontaneous phase 4 depolarisation in tissue that should be quiescent. Seen in ischaemia, catecholamine excess and digoxin toxicity
Triggered activity: afterdepolarisations dependent on a preceding beat. Early afterdepolarisations cause torsades de pointes; delayed afterdepolarisations arise from calcium overload

sections.heading: A bedside classification
facts: Is it fast or slow? Above 100 or below 60 beats per minute
Is the QRS narrow or wide? Narrow means supraventricular origin; wide means ventricular origin or aberrant conduction
Is it regular or irregular?
Is the patient stable or unstable? Instability — hypotension, ischaemia, heart failure, altered consciousness — mandates immediate electrical treatment
Irregularly irregular with no P waves is atrial fibrillation until proven otherwise
A wide-complex tachycardia is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise

pearls: The AV node is deliberately slow — that delay is what allows the atria to finish emptying.
The His–Purkinje system is deliberately fast — that speed is what gives a narrow QRS and efficient contraction.
Adenosine both terminates node-dependent tachycardias and unmasks atrial arrhythmias — it is diagnostic as well as therapeutic.
Never give AV nodal blockers in pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Always look for reversible triggers: ischaemia, electrolytes, drugs, thyroid disease and hypoxia.

title: Heart Failure Principles
summary: Classification, the neurohormonal cycle, and why guideline-directed therapy changes outcome rather than just symptoms.

rows: The strongest evidence base for disease-modifying therapy
Requires objective evidence of raised filling pressures

sections.heading: The neurohormonal cycle
sections.body: The mechanisms that defend perfusion acutely are the same ones that destroy the heart chronically. Understanding this single idea explains almost all of heart failure pharmacology.
facts: Reduced output unloads the baroreceptors, increasing sympathetic outflow
Sympathetic activation raises rate, contractility and afterload — and chronic catecholamine exposure is myocyte-toxic
Reduced renal perfusion activates renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone
Angiotensin II and aldosterone directly promote hypertrophy and fibrosis
Salt and water retention raises preload, but the flattened Starling curve converts this into congestion rather than output
Natriuretic peptides oppose this but are progressively overwhelmed — and are what we measure diagnostically

rows: At risk; no structural disease, no symptoms
Structural disease with current or prior symptoms

sections.heading: Common precipitants of decompensation
facts: Non-adherence to medication or dietary salt and fluid advice
Arrhythmia, particularly new atrial fibrillation
Myocardial ischaemia or infarction
Infection and sepsis
Uncontrolled hypertension
Anaemia, thyroid disease and iron deficiency
NSAIDs, corticosteroids and some calcium channel blockers
Excess alcohol and worsening renal function

pearls: Normal natriuretic peptides in an untreated, symptomatic patient make heart failure very unlikely.
Diuretics make patients feel better; neurohormonal blockade makes them live longer.
An S3 and a raised JVP are among the most informative bedside findings.
Always ask what precipitated this decompensation — there is almost always an answer.
Heart failure is a syndrome, not a diagnosis: the underlying cause must always be sought.

title: Valvular Heart Disease
summary: Severity thresholds, the physiology of pressure versus volume loading, and what determines the timing of intervention.

rows: Concentric hypertrophy — sarcomeres in parallel, thick wall, small cavity
Eccentric hypertrophy — sarcomeres in series, dilated cavity

table.caption: Commonly cited thresholds for severe disease; always confirm against current guidelines
rows: Area < 1.0 cm²; mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg; peak velocity ≥ 4 m/s
Effective regurgitant orifice ≥ 0.4 cm²; regurgitant volume ≥ 60 mL

sections.heading: Timing intervention
facts: Symptoms are the strongest single trigger in stenotic lesions, particularly aortic stenosis
In regurgitant lesions, ventricular size and function often deteriorate before symptoms — so surveillance measurements matter
Exercise testing can unmask symptoms in patients who have unconsciously limited their activity
Repair is preferred over replacement where a durable repair is achievable, particularly for the mitral valve
Decisions are made by a multidisciplinary heart team weighing anatomy, risk, life expectancy and patient preference

sections.heading: Acute versus chronic regurgitation
sections.body: The same lesion behaves entirely differently depending on how quickly it develops. Chronic regurgitation allows the receiving chamber to dilate and stay compliant, so pressures remain modest and patients stay asymptomatic for years. Acute regurgitation confronts a normal-sized, non-compliant chamber, so pressures rise abruptly, producing pulmonary oedema and shock — often with an unimpressive murmur.

pearls: Pressure overload thickens; volume overload dilates.
Loud murmurs are not necessarily severe, and severe lesions are not necessarily loud.
In aortic stenosis the ventricle is preload-dependent — beware vasodilators and hypovolaemia.
Low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis can conceal severe disease behind a reassuring gradient.
Rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation requires warfarin, not a DOAC.

title: Cardiovascular Examination
summary: A structured bedside examination and the signs that genuinely change your differential.

sections.heading: Sequence
facts: General inspection: comfort at rest, breathlessness, cachexia, cyanosis, scars, pacemaker box
Hands: clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions, tar staining, peripheral cyanosis
Pulse: rate, rhythm, character and volume; radioradial and radiofemoral delay; blood pressure in both arms
Face and neck: malar flush, xanthelasma, corneal arcus, conjunctival pallor; jugular venous pressure and waveform
Praecordium: inspect for scars and visible pulsation; palpate the apex beat, heaves and thrills
Auscultate all four areas with diaphragm and bell, plus axilla and carotids, with positional manoeuvres
Complete: lung bases, sacral and ankle oedema, liver, peripheral pulses, and a urine dipstick where relevant

rows: Rapid rise and fall, wide pulse pressure
Inspiratory fall in systolic pressure > 10 mmHg

sections.heading: Jugular venous pressure
facts: Measured as vertical height above the sternal angle with the patient at 45 degrees; normal is 3 cm or less
Distinguish from the carotid: the JVP has a double waveform, is non-palpable, varies with position and respiration, and is obliterated by light pressure
Elevated with a normal waveform: right heart failure, fluid overload
Giant v waves: tricuspid regurgitation
Cannon a waves: atrioventricular dissociation, as in complete heart block
Kussmaul's sign — inspiratory rise: constrictive pericarditis, right ventricular infarction, restrictive cardiomyopathy

sections.heading: The apex beat
facts: Normally in the fifth left intercostal space in the midclavicular line
Displaced and diffuse: ventricular dilatation
Sustained and heaving but undisplaced: pressure overload with concentric hypertrophy
Tapping: palpable loud first heart sound in mitral stenosis
Double impulse: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Impalpable: obesity, emphysema, pericardial effusion or dextrocardia

pearls: The JVP is the most information-dense sign in cardiovascular examination — spend time learning it.
Always feel both radial pulses and both femoral pulses, and check blood pressure in both arms.
Position matters: left lateral for mitral stenosis, sitting forward in expiration for aortic regurgitation.
Look at the patient from the end of the bed before you touch them.
Examination findings guide investigation — they rarely replace it.

title: Cardiovascular Imaging
summary: What each modality actually shows, what it does well, and when to choose it.

rows: First-line structure and function, valves, effusion, ventricular size
Operator- and window-dependent; limited posterior structures
Left atrial appendage, prosthetic valves, endocarditis, procedural guidance
Volumes, mass, tissue characterisation, scar and infiltration
Coronary anatomy, calcium score, structural planning
Radiation; contrast; limited by heart rate and calcium
Definitive coronary anatomy with physiology and intervention

sections.heading: Echocardiography essentials
facts: Standard views: parasternal long and short axis, apical four-, two- and three-chamber, subcostal, suprasternal
Ejection fraction is most commonly estimated by the biplane method of discs (modified Simpson's)
Doppler measures velocity; the simplified Bernoulli equation (pressure gradient ≈ 4v²) converts it to a gradient
Tricuspid regurgitant velocity plus estimated right atrial pressure gives pulmonary artery systolic pressure
Diastolic function is assessed from E/A ratio, e′ velocity, E/e′, left atrial volume index and TR velocity
Strain imaging detects subclinical dysfunction before ejection fraction falls

rows: Subendocardial or transmural, in a coronary territory
Patchy, at right ventricular insertion points

pearls: Ask what question you want answered before choosing the test.
Echocardiography answers most cardiology questions and should usually come first.
Cardiac MRI is the reference standard for volumes and the only routine way to characterise myocardial tissue.
A calcium score of zero is a powerful negative predictor in stable chest pain.
Imaging findings must always be interpreted alongside the clinical picture.

title: Cardiovascular Pharmacology
summary: Drug classes by mechanism, the haemodynamic lever each one pulls, and the effects that show up in exams and on the ward.

rows: Block angiotensin II formation or action
Heart failure, hypertension, post-infarction, proteinuric kidney disease
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Reduce rate, contractility and renin release
Renal glucose and sodium excretion; pleiotropic cardiorenal effects
Heart failure across the EF spectrum, diabetes, CKD
Dihydropyridines dilate vessels; non-dihydropyridines slow the AV node
Sodium channel, moderate block; prolongs repolarisation
Sodium channel, weak block; shortens repolarisation

sections.heading: Effects worth remembering
facts: ACE inhibitors: dry cough from bradykinin, hyperkalaemia, angioedema; avoid in pregnancy and bilateral renal artery stenosis
Beta-blockers: fatigue, bradycardia; introduce in stable heart failure and uptitrate slowly
Amiodarone: thyroid, pulmonary, hepatic, corneal and skin effects; requires structured monitoring
Digoxin: narrow therapeutic index; toxicity worsened by hypokalaemia; causes visual disturbance and arrhythmia
Statins: myalgia and, rarely, myopathy; check for interactions
Verapamil and diltiazem: negatively inotropic — avoid in significant systolic dysfunction, and never combine intravenously with a beta-blocker
Flecainide: avoid in structural heart disease and ischaemia

pearls: For every drug, ask which haemodynamic lever it pulls: preload, afterload, rate or contractility.
Diuretics relieve congestion; neurohormonal blockade modifies the disease.
Nitrates act mainly on veins — they reduce preload, which is how they relieve congestion and angina.
Aspirin is not adequate for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation.
Always check renal function and potassium when starting or uptitrating RAAS-acting drugs.

title: Interventional Cardiology
summary: What happens in the catheterisation laboratory: access, coronary intervention, structural procedures and their complications.

sections.heading: Vascular access
facts: Radial access is now the default for coronary procedures — lower bleeding and vascular complications, and earlier mobilisation
Femoral access is used for large-bore procedures such as transcatheter valve implantation and mechanical support
Allen's or Barbeau testing has historically been used to assess dual palmar supply before radial access
Ultrasound guidance reduces complications for femoral and venous access
Venous access via the femoral or jugular vein is used for right heart catheterisation and electrophysiology

sections.heading: Coronary intervention
facts: Diagnostic angiography defines anatomy; physiology (FFR or iFR) determines functional significance of intermediate lesions
Intravascular imaging — IVUS and OCT — assesses plaque, vessel sizing and stent optimisation
Balloon angioplasty followed by drug-eluting stent implantation is standard for most lesions
Calcified lesions may require rotational or orbital atherectomy, or intravascular lithotripsy
Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy in STEMI when it can be delivered within recommended times
Dual antiplatelet therapy after stenting, with duration individualised by ischaemic and bleeding risk

rows: Selected severe mitral regurgitation at high surgical risk
AF with a long-term contraindication to anticoagulation
Significant shunt, or selected cryptogenic stroke
Right ventricular outflow tract dysfunction after repair

sections.heading: Complications to know
facts: Access site: haematoma, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula, retroperitoneal haemorrhage, radial artery occlusion
Coronary: dissection, perforation, no-reflow, side-branch occlusion, stent thrombosis and restenosis
Systemic: contrast-associated acute kidney injury, contrast allergy, atheroembolism, stroke
Structural procedures: conduction block requiring pacing (particularly after TAVI), paravalvular leak, device embolisation, tamponade
Radiation exposure to both patient and operator

pearls: An angiogram shows the lumen, not the plaque — this is why intravascular imaging and physiology matter.
Not every stenosis needs a stent; functional significance should guide intervention in stable disease.
In STEMI, door-to-balloon time is the number that matters most.
Conduction block after TAVI reflects the bundle of His lying just beneath the aortic valve.
Radial access has substantially reduced bleeding complications and is the default for coronary work.
